#103787. Your Brain on Grief, Your Heart on Healing

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2850 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Themarginalian ↗ Open Full Page

Your Brain on Grief, Your Heart on Healing

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2850 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Themarginalian

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “‘Tis good — the looking back on Grief,” Emily Dickinson wrote as she calibrated love and loss.
  • In a recent development, and besides, what does it mean to lose a love anyway?
  • On the one hand, we lose people all the time — to death, to distance, to differences; from the brain’s point of view, these varieties of loss differ not by kind but only by degree, triggering the same neural circuitry, producing sorrow along a spectrum of intensity shaped by the level of closeness and the finality of the loss.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“‘Tis good — the looking back on Grief,” Emily Dickinson wrote as she calibrated love and loss. But she did not mean that it is good to ruminate and wallow — Dickinson so deftly played with the surface of meaning, so delighted in startling us into a flinch or furrow before plunging us into the deeper truths she fathomed. She meant, I think, that a love lost is grieved forever, whatever the nature of the loss — this she knew, and turned the ongoingness of it into a lifetime of art — but by looking back, we are reminded over and over that the sharp edge of grief does smooth over time, that today’s blunt ache is worlds apart from the first stabs, until grief becomes, as Abraham Lincoln wrote in his stirring letter of consolation to a bereaved young woman, “a sad sweet feeling in your heart, of a purer and holier sort than you have known before.”.

In a recent development, and besides, what does it mean to lose a love anyway? We never lose people, not really. I don’t mean this in some mystical sense — let there be no confusion about what actually happens when we die. I don’t even mean it in the poetic sense. I am speaking strictly from the point of view of the mind emerging from the dazzling materiality of the brain — that majestic cathedral of cortex and synapse shaping every thought we have and every feeling we tremble with.

I am speaking of the paradox inside the brain:.

On the one hand, we lose people all the time — to death, to distance, to differences; from the brain’s point of view, these varieties of loss differ not by kind but only by degree, triggering the same neural circuitry, producing sorrow along a spectrum of intensity shaped by the level of closeness and the finality of the loss.

Sources indicate that on the other hand, no person we have loved is ever fully gone. When they die or vanish, they are physically no longer present, but their personhood permeates our synapses with memories and habits of mind, saturates an all-pervading atmosphere of feeling we don’t just carry with us all the time but live and breathe inside. Or the opposite happens, which is its own devastation — the physical body remains present, but the person we have known and loved, that safehouse of shared memories and trust, is gone — lost to mental illness, to addiction, to neurodegenerative disease.

It has been revealed that in both cases, the brain is tasked with the slow, painful work of reconstituting its map of the world, so that the world makes sense again without the beloved person in it. Mapping, in fact, is not a mere metaphor but what is actually going on in the brain, since our orientation in spacetime and our autonoeic consciousness — the capacity for mental self-representation — share a cortical region.

Where the missed and missing person goes on the map, how the remapping actually unfolds, and what it takes to redraw the map in such a way that the world feels whole again are the questions coursing through The Grieving Brain: The Surprising Science of How We Learn from Love and Loss (public library) by neuroscientist Mary-Frances O’Connor — a pioneer in fMRI research since the technology first became available, who has devoted a quarter century to studying the particular neurophysiology of grief. She writes:.

In a recent development, the brain devotes lots of effort to mapping where our loved ones are while they are alive, so that we can find them when we need them. And the brain often prefers habits and predictions over new information. But it struggles to learn new information that cannot be ignored, like the absence of our loved one.

Recent findings suggest that grief is a heart-wrenchingly painful problem for the brain to solve, and grieving necessitates learning to live in the world with the absence of someone you love deeply, who is ingrained in your understanding of the world. This means that for the brain, your loved one is simultaneously gone and also everlasting, and you are walking through two worlds at the same time. You are navigating your life despite the fact that they have been stolen from you, a premise that makes no sense, and that is both confusing and upsetting.

Making an important distinction between grief (“the intense emotion that crashes over you like a wave, completely overwhelming, unable to be ignored”) and grieving (an ongoing process punctuated by recurring moments of grief but stringing the moments into a larger trajectory), O’Connor adds:.

Grieving requires the difficult task of throwing out the map we have used to navigate our lives together and transforming our relationship with this person who has died. Grieving, or learning to live a meaningful life without our loved one, is ultimately a type of learning. Because learning is something we do our whole lives, seeing grieving as a type of learning may make it feel more familiar and understandable and give us the patience to allow this remarkable process to unfold.

Recent findings suggest that grief never ends, and it is a natural response to loss. You will experience pangs of grief over this specific person forever. You will have discrete moments that overwhelm you, even years after the death when you have restored your life to a meaningful, fulfilling experience. But… even if the feeling of grief is the same, your relationship to the feeling changes. Feeling grief years after your loss may make you doubt whether you have really adapted. If you think of the emotion and the process of adaptation as two different things, however, then it isn’t a problem that you experience grief even when you have been grieving for a long time.

Although volumes have been written about the psychology, philosophy, and poetics of grief — none more piercing than the Joan Didion classic, none more practical than Seneca’s advice to his bereaved mother — there is something singularly revealing about exploring grief from the point of view of the brain beneath the mind, which must begin at the developmental beginning. Childhood — the brain’s most fertile growth period, when most of its major infrastructure is laid out — is also our training ground for loss. Every time we are separated from our primary caregivers, we experience scale-models of loss; every time they return, we learn that the loss of their presence is not a loss of their person, of their love. (A pause worth taking: every abandonment is a miniature of grief.).

In those formative attachments, we also learn the role we ourselves play in the relationship. Because, in building its relational world-map, the brain is constantly computing our loved ones’ position in three dimensions — time, space, and closeness, also known as psychological distance — we learn the causal link between our behavior and a caregiver’s position in the closeness dimension, just like we learn the causal link between our bodily movements and our position in space. When there is secure attachment, the child learns that throughout various surface disruptions, situational factors, and passing emotional weather patterns, there is a steadfast underlying closeness. O’Connor writes:.

Closeness is partially under our control, and we learn how to maintain and nurture this closeness, but we also trust those who love us to maintain that closeness as well.

The obvious — and heartbreaking — corollary is that children who grow up without secure attachment experience the pangs of miniature grief much more readily throughout life, with each departure of a loved one, however temporary, because trusting a continuity of closeness does not come naturally to us. But no matter the formative experience of closeness, human beings are universally undone by the death of someone close — the final abandonment, at once the most abstract and the most absolute absence, in which our brains simply cannot compute the total removal of a person so proximate and key from the fabric of psychological spacetime.

Citing the disoriented devastation of a woman ghosted by a lover, O’Connor notes that “ghosting” is the neurologically appropriate word-choice for such abandonments — studied under fMRI, the brain of a person who has lost a loved one to “ghosting” behaves much the same way as the brain of a person who has lost a loved one to death, the mental map suddenly crumbled and torn to pieces. O’Connor describes the strange yet strangely sensical way in which the brain copes with this incomprehensible disruption of reality:.

According to recent reports, if your brain cannot comprehend that something as abstract as death has happened, it cannot understand where the deceased is in space and time, or why they are not here, now, and close. From your brain’s perspective, ghosting is exactly what happens when a loved one dies. As far as the brain is concerned, they have not died. The loved one has, with no explanation, stopped returning our calls — stopped communicating with us altogether. How could someone who loves us do that? They have become distant, or unbelievably mean, and that is infuriating. Your brain doesn’t understand why; it doesn’t understand that dimensions can simply disappear. If they don’t feel close, then they just feel distant, and you want to fix it rather than believe they are permanently gone. This (mis)belief leads to an intense upwelling of emotions.

Sources indicate that if a person we love is missing, then our brain assumes they are far away and will be found later. The idea that the person is simply no longer in this dimensional world, that there are no here, now, and close dimensions, is not logical.

Drawing on brain imaging studies, she adds:.

The ephemeral sense of closeness with our loved ones exists in the physical, tangible hardware of our brain.

The particular bit of hardware is the brain’s posterior cingulate cortex — our built-in GPS of love. Scanning the environment and processing innumerable bits of sensory information, the PCC is constantly calibrating and recalibrating the psychological distance between us and the people we love, tightening the bond the closer we feel and loosening it when we sense distancing. Death turns the GPS into a crude compass trying to orient to an all-pervading, ever-shifting magnetic field suddenly bereft of its true north. O’Connor writes:.

According to recent reports, after the death of a loved one, the incoming messages seem scrambled for a while. At times, closeness with our deceased loved one feels incredibly visceral, as though they are present in the room, here and now. At other times, the string seems to have fallen off the board — not shorter or longer than it was before, but simply stolen from us entirely.

This confusion is so fundamental and so primal, so beyond the reach of reason, that it befalls minds indiscriminately along the spectrum of intelligence and self-awareness — a reality most clearly and devastatingly evinced in the extraordinary love letter Richard Feynman wrote to his wife 488 days after her death and 6,994 days before he won the Nobel Prize in Physics.

But O’Connor notes that while Western physicians long believed such continuing bonds across the life-death divide to be a symptom of poor coping with grief that makes for poorer bonds with the living, recent research drawing on various grief rituals and customs from cultures around the world has demonstrated that such ongoing inner dialogue with the dead might actually enrich our relationships with the living and allow us to show up for them in a fuller, more openhearted way. She writes:.

Our understanding of ourselves changes as we gain wisdom through experience. Our relationships with our living loved ones can grow more compassionate and resonant with gratitude as we age. We can also allow our interactions with our beloved ones who are gone to grow and change, even if only in our minds. This transformation of our relationship with them can affect our capacity to live fully in the present, and to create aspirations for a meaningful future. It can also help us to feel more connected to them, to the best parts of them… Their absence from our physical world does not make our relationship to them any less valuable.

In a recent development, instead of imagining an alternate what if reality, we must learn to be connected to them with our feet planted firmly in the present moment. This transformed relationship is dynamic, ever-changing, in the way that any loving relationship is ever-changing across months and years. Our relationship with our deceased loved one must reflect who we are now, with the experience, and perhaps even the wisdom, we have gained through grieving. We must learn to restore a meaningful life.

According to recent reports, the greatest challenge, of course, is the perennial challenge of the human mind — how to integrate seemingly contradictory needs or ideas in such a way that they coexist harmoniously, perhaps even magnify each other, rather than cancel each other out. Without such integration, any latest relationship can feel like a threat to this ongoing inner bond with the dead, undamming a flood of grief at the notion of emotional erasure: grief for the grief itself, for that outstretched hand holding on to the gone and to ourselves at the same time, to the map as it used to be. This is a fear so understandable as to cusp on the universal. It is also — and this might be the most assuring part of O’Connor’s research — a neurophysiologically misplaced fear. Within the brain, every person we love leaves a tangible, structural imprint, encoded in synapses that can never be vanquished or replaced by new and different love. Because that bond — like every bond, like every idea, like the universe itself — was “only ever conjured up in the mind,” it is there too that it always lives, unassailable by other minds and other events.

Gaining a latest relationship is simply not going to fill the hole that exists. Here is the key — the point of new roles and new relationships is not to fill the hole. Expecting that they will can only lead to disappointment.

The point is that if we are living in the present, we need to have someone who loves us and cares for us, and we need someone to love and care for as well. The only way to enjoy a fulfilling relationship in the future, however, is to start one in the present. If we can imagine a future in which we are loved, then we must start a relationship that eventually will become key to us in a way that is different from our previous relationship, but rewarding and sustaining.

Understood this way, then, the ongoing relationship with the gone is a lavishment to other loves, for it has made us exactly who we are — the person doing the loving, the person being loved, the mapmaker of present and possible worlds. O’Connor offers neural affirmation for this poetic aspiration:.

Recent findings suggest that after a loved one dies, they are clearly no longer with us in the physical world, which each day proves to us. On the other hand, they are not gone, because they are with us in our brain and in our mind. The physical makeup of our brain — the structure of our neurons — has been changed by them. In this sense, you could say that a piece of them physically lives on. That piece is the neural connections protected within our skull, and these neural connections survive in physical form even after a loved one’s death. So, they are not entirely “out there,” and they are not entirely “in here,” either. You are not one, not two. That is because the love between two people, that unmistakable but usually indescribable property, occurs between two people. Once we have known love, we can bring it into our awareness, we can feel it emerge and emanate from us. This experience reaches beyond the love for the flesh and bones of the person we once knew on this earthly plane. Now loving is an attribute of us, regardless of who we share it with, regardless of what is given to us in return. This is a transcendent experience, a felt sense of being loving without needing anything in return. In the very best moments together, we learned to love and to be loved. Because of our bonded experience, that loved one and that loving are a part of us now, to call up and act on as we see fit in the present and the future.

Complement The Grieving Brain with a mathematician’s geometric model for living with grief and this soulful animated film of “Dirge Without Music” by Edna St. Vincent Millay — the most beautiful homily on the emotional paradox of loss I know — then revisit Nick Cave’s life-honed wisdom on grief as a portal to greater aliveness.

#103786. Scientists discover a natural compound that could protect the brain from too much salt

Scientists discover a natural compound that could protect the brain from too much salt

📅 18 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1278 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, consuming too much salt can affect more than blood pressure.
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers in Japan have identified a promising possibility in LPC70, a compound derived from soy.
  • How a Soy Compound May Counter the Effects of Excess Salt.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, consuming too much salt can affect more than blood pressure. Growing evidence suggests that excessive salt intake may also interfere with memory, thinking, and emotional well-being. High salt (HS) consumption is already a major public health concern because of its connection to hypertension, but its potential effects on the brain make finding ways to reduce the damage even more vital.

Recent findings suggest that researchers in Japan have identified a promising possibility in LPC70, a compound derived from soy. Previous research found that this ingredient could reduce high blood pressure and cognitive problems associated with a high-salt diet (HSD) in mice. The latest study takes a closer look at how it works, revealing that the compound influences important chemical signals in the brain and kidneys.

How a Soy Compound May Counter the Effects of Excess Salt.

Industry observers note that the research centers on prostaglandins (PGs), signaling molecules made from a fatty acid called arachidonic acid (AA). These substances act much like local hormones, helping regulate essential functions throughout the body.

It has been revealed that in the cardiovascular system, prostaglandins help control blood pressure by balancing the widening and narrowing of blood vessels. Their effects in the brain are more complicated. Depending on which receptors they activate, they can trigger signals that either protect nerve cells or contribute to harmful processes, potentially affecting memory, thinking, and emotional responses.

It has been revealed that LPC70 is a form of soy lysolecithin in which lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) accounts for more than 70% of the phospholipids. Although earlier experiments revealed that LPC70 could ease salt-related hypertension and cognitive difficulties, scientists had not fully understood the mechanisms responsible, particularly its influence on prostaglandin signaling.

Industry observers note that to investigate, a research team led by Professor Akihiro Mouri and Dr. Hisayoshi Kubota, working with Dr. Kazuhiro Kagotani, examined how LPC70 affected these signaling pathways in mice consuming a high-salt diet.

Dr. Kubota, the study's first author, played a central role in the experiments. He assessed blood pressure, monitored behavioral changes, and analyzed molecular activity associated with prostaglandins. His work helped clarify how LPC70 produces different effects in the organs involved in salt-related cardiovascular and cognitive problems.

Prof. Mouri and Dr. Kubota are affiliated with the Department of Regulatory Science for Evaluation and Development of Pharmaceuticals & Devices at Fujita Health University Graduate School of Medical Science, as well as the International Center for Brain Science (ICBS) at Fujita Health University in Japan. Dr. Kagotani is affiliated with Tsuji Oil Mills Co., Ltd, in Japan and the Tsuji Health and Beauty Science Laboratory at Mie University, Japan.

The findings were released online on May 14, 2026, and published in Volume 197 of Neurochemistry International on July 1, 2026.

It has been revealed that "We wanted to understand the role of LPC70 in coordinating changes in PG signaling across organ systems," mentioned Prof. Mouri. "Our study originated from a collaborative research project with Tsuji Oil Mills Co., Ltd, a manufacturer that develops naturally derived food ingredients," he added.

Soy Compound Improves Blood Pressure and Memory in Mice.

Recent findings suggest that as expected, mice that consumed a high-salt diet developed elevated blood pressure. However, the consequences extended beyond their cardiovascular health.

The animals also became less socially interactive and had difficulty recognizing objects they had encountered before, indicating problems with memory. Interestingly, their general movement and anxiety-like behavior demonstrated no substantial changes. This pattern suggests that excessive salt selectively disrupted more complex cognitive and social functions rather than causing widespread behavioral impairment.

When researchers supplemented the animals' diets with LPC70, several of these effects were reduced. Blood pressure improved, and the mice performed better on tests of social interaction and object recognition memory.

These improvements prompted the researchers to examine what was happening inside the animals' kidneys and brains.

Different Protective Effects in the Kidneys and Brain.

According to recent reports, in the kidneys, a high-salt diet increased the expression of two components involved in prostaglandin signaling: cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) and the PGE2 receptor EP3. Both may contribute to the development of high blood pressure associated with excessive salt consumption.

LPC70 reduced these salt-related increases, suggesting that the compound helps correct changes in kidney signaling that can interfere with normal blood pressure regulation.

The researchers found a different response in the prefrontal cortex, a brain region essential for thinking, memory, and social behavior.

Recent findings suggest that excess salt reduced the expression of the PGD2 receptor DP1, which plays a role in protective and anti-inflammatory signaling in the brain. LPC70 restored expression of this receptor without changing DP2, another receptor associated with potentially harmful effects on nerve cells.

According to recent reports, this distinction is important because it suggests that LPC70 does not simply increase or suppress all prostaglandin activity. Instead, it may selectively favor signaling pathways that help protect the brain, potentially explaining the improvements in memory and social behavior observed in the mice.

A Surprising Change in Chemical Signaling.

The team also discovered an unexpected change involving arachidonic acid, the fatty acid the body uses to produce prostaglandins.

Recent findings suggest that mice consuming excess salt had lower levels of circulating arachidonic acid. Yet when they received LPC70, levels of prostaglandins derived from this fatty acid, including PGE2 and PGD2, increased.

This seemingly contradictory result suggests that LPC70 may help the body use available arachidonic acid more efficiently to produce prostaglandins under high-salt conditions.

Taken together, the findings reveal a coordinated but highly selective response. In the kidneys, LPC70 appears to suppress signaling changes associated with hypertension. In the brain, it restores signaling linked to protection against inflammation and damage.

The compound's effects therefore depend on both the organ involved and the specific prostaglandin receptors being regulated.

Could Soy-Based Ingredients Help Protect Against Excess Salt?

The results suggest that LPC70 could eventually become a useful functional food ingredient for reducing some of the health consequences of excessive salt intake.

Its ability to improve blood pressure and cognitive performance in mice raises the possibility that it could support cardiovascular and brain health, particularly among people whose diets contain high amounts of salt.

However, the findings come from animal experiments, and further clinical studies are needed to determine whether the same benefits occur in humans.

"Our study elucidates LPC70's role in PG signaling, laying the groundwork for future clinical research and dietary interventions aimed at reducing hypertension-related cognitive decline and promoting healthy aging globally," concluded Prof. Mouri.

The research provides a clearer picture of how a soy-derived compound can influence the body's response to excessive salt, opening new possibilities for nutritional approaches to protecting long-term health.

The study received support through Grants-in-Aid for Scientific Research from the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science (JSPS: 20K07931, 22K07606, 22K11891, and 23H02843).

Additional support came from the Fujita Mind-Brain Research & Innovation Center for Drug Generation (Fujita Mind-BRIDGe) through Japan's Peak Research Universities (J-PEAKS) Program (JPJS00420240019), along with the Japan Science and Technology Agency FOREST Program (JPMJFR215H).

Tsuji Oil Mills Co., Ltd. provided funding for the research. Grants and other support were also supplied by the Education and Research Facility of Animal Models for Human Diseases at Fujita Health University, the Smoking Research Foundation, and the Takeda Science Foundation.

Magic mushroom ingredient takes the fight out of aggressive fish

📅 18 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1026 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that psilocybin, the psychedelic substance found in more than 200 species of mushrooms, appears to have an unexpected effect on aggressive fish.
  • In a recent development, to investigate this question, researchers in Canada examined the effects of psilocybin on the amphibious mangrove rivulus fish (Kryptolebias marmoratus).
  • "We show that an acute, low dose of psilocybin significantly reduces activity and aggressive attack behavior during social interactions in adult mangrove rivulus fish, a species that is naturally highly aggressive," remarked first author Dayna Forsyth, a research associate and former MSc student at Acadia University in Nova Scotia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that psilocybin, the psychedelic substance found in more than 200 species of mushrooms, appears to have an unexpected effect on aggressive fish. Most mushrooms containing this compound belong to the gilled mushroom genus Psilocybe. In mammals, psilocybin interacts with serotonin receptors in the brain, influencing emotions and behaviors such as mood, appetite, and aggression. However, scientists still know relatively little about how the substance affects social interactions among animals.

In a recent development, to investigate this question, researchers in Canada examined the effects of psilocybin on the amphibious mangrove rivulus fish (Kryptolebias marmoratus). Their findings, published in Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience, suggest that even a brief exposure to a low dose can significantly reduce aggressive behavior without disrupting normal social interactions.

"We show that an acute, low dose of psilocybin significantly reduces activity and aggressive attack behavior during social interactions in adult mangrove rivulus fish, a species that is naturally highly aggressive," remarked first author Dayna Forsyth, a research associate and former MSc student at Acadia University in Nova Scotia.

"These findings provide the first evidence that psilocybin can selectively reduce escalated aggression in a vertebrate model without suppressing social interaction," added senior author Dr. Suzie Currie, a biologist at The University of British Columbia.

Why Scientists Studied Aggressive Mangrove Rivulus Fish.

Mangrove rivulus fish are naturally combative, particularly when they encounter another member of their species. Their aggressive responses are easy to recognize and measure, allowing researchers to detect even small changes in behavior.

These fish also have an unusual reproductive ability. They can fertilize themselves, producing offspring that are genetically identical. This makes them especially useful for experiments because scientists can minimize genetic variation and more confidently attribute behavioral differences to psilocybin rather than inherited traits.

Recent findings suggest that for the experiment, the researchers worked with three genetically distinct lines of fish bred in the laboratory. One group received psilocybin, another provided the fish used to provoke social interactions, and the third helped researchers measure how much psilocybin entered and accumulated in the animals' bodies.

Industry observers note that the researchers first established a baseline for each fish's behavior. They placed a fish into a tank already occupied by another fish, with the two separated by a fiberglass mesh barrier and an opaque cover. The mesh prevented physical contact while allowing the fish to see and smell each other once the cover was removed.

After allowing five minutes for the fish to adjust to their shared environment, the team removed the opaque cover and recorded their interactions.

The following day, 24 hours after the initial observation, the researchers placed the same fish in water containing dissolved psilocybin. Following 20 minutes of exposure, they returned it to the tank with the same fish it had encountered previously. The opaque cover was then removed again so the researchers could observe any changes in behavior.

Magic Mushroom Compound Reduces Aggressive Attacks.

The results revealed a striking change. Fish exposed to psilocybin moved around less and displayed fewer bursts of aggressive swimming than fish that had not received the substance.

To assess these changes, the scientists measured overall activity (time spent moving) and several signs of aggression (including swimming bursts). These rapid bursts are particularly notable because they indicate that an encounter is escalating toward an attack, even when the fish cannot make physical contact.

"Swimming bursts are high-energy attack behaviors that represent an escalation of aggression towards the stimulus fish without making physical contact," explained Currie. "Other types of aggressive behaviors, like head-on displays, are more about communication and social assessment and require very little energy.".

Interestingly, psilocybin did not suppress every form of aggressive or social behavior. While the fish became less likely to engage in intense, energy-demanding attacks, their less physically demanding social displays remained largely unchanged.

Recent findings suggest that "Psilocybin's calming effect appears to selectively reduce energetically costly, escalated behaviors while lower-energy social display behaviors remained largely unchanged," remarked Forsyth. "This suggests that this compound can selectively dampen escalated social conflict rather than shutting down behavior altogether.".

Sources indicate that the compound also reduced general activity. When placed alongside another member of their species, fish treated with psilocybin spent less time swimming than untreated controls.

Together, these findings suggest that psilocybin may influence specific aspects of aggressive behavior rather than simply making animals less responsive to their surroundings.

What the Findings Could Mean for Psychedelic Research.

The researchers believe animal studies like this one could eventually help scientists better understand how psychedelic compounds influence behavior and identify possible directions for therapeutic research.

By examining which social responses are most sensitive to psilocybin, researchers may be able to uncover biological mechanisms that are difficult to investigate directly in people. Such insights could ultimately inform studies of potential clinical applications.

Sources indicate that however, the team emphasized that the findings should not be interpreted as evidence of a treatment for aggression in humans. The experiment involved fish, did not evaluate any clinical intervention, and cannot establish whether similar effects would occur in people.

Recent findings suggest that there are also important questions about how long the calming effect lasts. The researchers examined only single doses and short exposure periods. They did not investigate repeated treatments, long-term behavioral changes, or whether the fish might adapt to the substance over time.

Additional experiments will be necessary to determine whether psilocybin's ability to reduce aggressive attacks can persist beyond the brief period examined in this study.

In a recent development, "Future studies can build on this work to explore how psilocybin alters neural signaling, which serotonin pathways are involved, and why some aspects of social behavior are affected while others are not," concluded Currie. "These are questions that are difficult or impossible to answer directly in humans.".

#103784. Tech Report: Modern neuroscience is rediscovering a surprising idea freud had 130 years ago

📅 19 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1325 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Modern neuroscience is rediscovering a surprising idea freud had 130 years ago

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1325 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What if the human brain works in ways that Sigmund Freud began describing more than 130 years ago?
  • Published in the scientific journal Entropy, the paper explores connections between Freud's original theories, later developments in psychoanalysis, and a modern approach to brain research known as the prediction paradigm.
  • This approach describes the brain as a prediction machine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What if the human brain works in ways that Sigmund Freud began describing more than 130 years ago? A latest scientific analysis suggests that some of his ideas about the mind share surprising similarities with one of the most influential theories in modern neuroscience.

Published in the scientific journal Entropy, the paper explores connections between Freud's original theories, later developments in psychoanalysis, and a modern approach to brain research known as the prediction paradigm.

This approach describes the brain as a prediction machine. Rather than simply responding to information from the outside world, the brain is constantly anticipating what will happen next. It then compares those expectations with incoming information from the senses and works to reduce any differences between what it predicted and what actually occurred.

Scientists believe this ongoing process plays a central role in how people perceive their surroundings, make decisions, behave, and regulate emotions.

Researchers Erik Stänicke, Bendik Hovet, and Line Indrevoll Stänicke, together with colleagues, argue that this modern understanding of brain function has crucial parallels with ideas that psychoanalysts have been developing for more than a century.

"For over 130 years, psychoanalysis has developed psychological theories about how predictions take place at a subjective level, which cognitive neuropsychology is now studying at a physiological level.".

How Freud's Ideas Connect to the Predictive Brain.

Although neuroscience and psychoanalysis approach the mind differently, the researchers suggest that both may be describing related processes.

Neuroscience examines the physical mechanisms behind thought and behavior, often using mathematical models to explain how the brain processes information. Psychoanalysis, which grew out of Freud's work, focuses more on unconscious mental processes, emotional experiences, and the ways past relationships influence present behavior.

In other words, one field investigates what happens inside the brain, while the other explores how those processes are experienced by the individual.

A particularly interesting connection involves the psychoanalytic concept of projection and the neuroscientific concept of prediction.

It has been revealed that in psychoanalysis, projection involves attributing feelings, intentions, or qualities to someone else. The researchers suggest that this resembles how the brain uses previously learned expectations to interpret upcoming experiences.

"When we attribute qualities, intentions or feelings to other people, our brain shapes our experience of the world in line with established expectations," says Stänicke.

In a recent development, for instance, someone who has repeatedly experienced rejection may become especially sensitive to signs that other people are rejecting them. Even an ambiguous remark or facial expression might be interpreted negatively because past experiences have shaped what the person expects.

Over time, these expectations can influence how someone approaches unfamiliar situations and forms upcoming relationships.

"This corresponds to the neuroscientific distinction between changing one's own predictions, perceptual inference, and the attempt to make the world conform to them, namely active inference.".

It has been revealed that perceptual inference refers to the way the brain interprets sensory information and updates its expectations in response. Active inference, by contrast, involves taking actions that help bring experiences into line with predictions or reduce uncertainty.

Recent findings suggest that together, these concepts help explain why people do not always experience the world as it objectively is. Their expectations can influence what they notice, how they interpret events, and how they respond.

Why the Brain Holds On to Negative Expectations.

The researchers believe the similarities between Freud's ideas and modern neuroscience could offer valuable insights into mental health disorders, particularly those involving deeply established patterns of thinking and behavior.

Both approaches portray the mind as constantly seeking stability and predictability. This tendency is related to homeostasis, the process through which a system maintains a relatively stable internal state.

According to recent reports, in the predictive brain model, reducing uncertainty is an crucial part of maintaining that stability. The brain relies on familiar expectations to make the world easier to understand, even when those expectations are inaccurate or no longer helpful.

"Psychoanalysts refer to the tendency in the mind to recreate familiar relational patterns, even when these are poorly adapted," claims Stänicke.

This could help explain why people sometimes repeat harmful patterns in relationships or continue interpreting situations negatively despite evidence that challenges their assumptions.

"Rigid and persistent symptoms, such as paranoid ideas or an internalized critical voice, may be stable but not very flexible prediction models," notes Stänicke.

"For example, there may be people who automatically expect criticism, rejection or hostility from others, and therefore interpret situations through this filter despite the fact that reality does not warrant it.".

Sources indicate that such expectations can become deeply entrenched because they make experiences feel familiar and predictable. Even when the resulting interpretation is distorted, maintaining an established mental model may feel less uncertain than changing it.

According to Stänicke, this offers a possible explanation for why some psychological symptoms can persist for years and why changing longstanding patterns of thought and behavior often requires considerable time.

The connection is particularly interesting because it suggests that some mental health difficulties may involve more than consciously held beliefs. They may also reflect deeply learned expectations that automatically shape emotional responses and interactions with others.

How Psychotherapy Could Help Change Deeply Rooted Patterns.

The researchers also highlight an notable distinction between what people consciously believe and what they have learned through experience.

"In addition, both models give us insight into how parts of our expectations of the outside world are not only anchored cognitively, but in procedural memory that is expressed in relational ways of being," he says.

According to recent reports, procedural memory is a type of long-term memory involved in learned habits and skills. It allows people to perform familiar actions without consciously thinking through every step.

In the context of relationships, the researchers suggest that a similar form of learning may help explain why certain emotional reactions and patterns of interaction become automatic.

Someone might intellectually understand that other people are not necessarily hostile or critical, for example, yet still instinctively respond as though rejection is inevitable.

These expectations are not simply thoughts that can be changed through reasoning. They can also be embedded in habitual ways of reacting to people and navigating relationships.

This distinction may help explain why psychotherapy sometimes needs to address personal relationships and emotional experiences rather than focusing only on conscious thoughts.

"Therefore, psychotherapy sometimes has to work relationally. For example, fresh experiences in the relationship between therapist and patient can gradually help to change entrenched relational patterns.".

Through repeated experiences that challenge familiar expectations, patients may gradually develop different ways of interpreting situations and relating to other people.

Bringing Freud's Psychoanalysis and Neuroscience Together.

The researchers argue that connecting psychoanalysis with modern predictive brain theory could benefit both fields.

Industry observers note that neuroscience may provide a biological framework for understanding processes that psychoanalysts have long described through subjective experience. At the same time, psychoanalytic theories may offer more detailed explanations of how expectations are experienced emotionally, interpreted personally, and expressed through relationships.

The proposed similarities do not establish that Freud's broader theories were correct. Instead, they suggest that two very different traditions of studying the mind may offer complementary ways of understanding some of the same psychological processes.

By examining both the brain's physical mechanisms and the individual's inner experience, researchers hope to develop a more complete understanding of human behavior and mental health.

"Bringing these two fields together can open up for a more holistic psychology, in which both neurological mechanisms and subjective experience are included. In this way, we can understand subjectivity in a more scientific manner.".

How Becoming a Parent Can Change Your Memories of Your Own Parents

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2233 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was around Christmas time when Emily* noticed that something was wrong.
  • Industry observers note that emily sought help from me in therapy just before Christmas when she realized that the prospect of spending the holidays with her parents was making it difficult for her to sleep and the few precious hours she had between feeds were taken up with anxious rumination.
  • In a recent development, I work a lot with mothers and birthing people in the perinatal phase, and the change they experience in their relationship with their parents is something that comes up very frequently.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was around Christmas time when Emily* noticed that something was wrong. She had just welcomed her second son in September and still felt emotionally raw from the experience. Part of Emily’s postpartum planning had revolved around having her mum look after her three-year-old while she took care of the new baby. But every time she visited her parents, something in her tensed up, her mind went foggy, and instead of feeling the safety and relaxation she had been craving, she felt on edge.

Industry observers note that emily sought help from me in therapy just before Christmas when she realized that the prospect of spending the holidays with her parents was making it difficult for her to sleep and the few precious hours she had between feeds were taken up with anxious rumination. She couldn’t make any sense of it. It was like a switch had flipped and the previously supportive, albeit slightly emotionally disconnected, relationship she had had with her parents was in pieces.

In a recent development, I work a lot with mothers and birthing people in the perinatal phase, and the change they experience in their relationship with their parents is something that comes up very frequently. Sometimes this change is positive, where they become more understanding of parents who were trying their best at the time. Sometimes it’s disorienting, like Emily’s, and the relationship seems to worsen. Either way, it’s vital to meet yourself with compassion and curiosity when unexpected feelings or memories resurface during this period of your life and try not to go through this transition on your own.

Recent findings suggest that emily came to see me for help with anxiety and insomnia, and a few sessions into our therapy she started to talk about memories that had been appearing for her, scenes from her childhood that suddenly had taken on upcoming meaning or had popped up out of nowhere. It was as if her memories had changed, which made Emily feel crazy and even more anxious because she felt like she couldn’t trust herself anymore.

In the crudest terms, we tend to think of memory as a filing cabinet—a place where scenes, facts, annoying songs, and embarrassing moments are stored to be recalled, like when we try to remember what we had for dinner last week or where we went on holiday three years ago.

When I talk about memory with my clients, they usually understand that it is not a perfect system, that it can alter over time and be very subjective. What is harder to convey is that decades of research suggest that memory is not in fact a filing cabinet or a library catalogue—it’s a construction. Every time I try to remember where we went on holiday three summers ago, my brain doesn’t retrieve but rather constructs a memory of our trip to Italy. That means that each time we recall something, that memory can change slightly or take on newly introduced meaning. Researchers Daniel L. Schacter and Donna Rose Addis found that, in fact, remembering and imagining look very similar in terms of activation in the brain.

Recent findings suggest that why does that matter? It can help make sense of what happened to Emily and what happens to many of my clients when they become parents and their relationships with their own parents change. Some of this is explained by a shift in roles: When a child becomes a parent, the dynamic of the child-parent relationship naturally has to change, which can be difficult for both parties. Grandparents and new parents might find it challenging to adapt to who is in charge and “who knows best.” But sometimes the difficulty is more subtle, and it’s related to memory.

Emily struggled because she had started to have visceral memories of herself at about three to five years old, even though she had never actively thought about her childhood much before. She associated that phase in her life with a feeling of paralysis that she couldn’t explain. She told me how exhausted she felt every time she left her parents’ house now, like she had been holding her breath for hours.

Emily knew from whispered family stories that her mother had dealt with bouts of depression through much of her childhood. She also knew that her parents’ marriage hadn’t always been as placid and quiet as it was now. She had always had memories of them fighting late at night but had never thought much of it. Now she remembered her mother in tears, shouting and doors slamming. She remembered hiding under her bed.

In a recent development, memory is heavily influenced by our current state of mind. Martin Conway, in his papers on autobiographical memory, explains that when we try to retrieve a memory or remember something spontaneously, we construct that memory in the moment, partly based on our current goals. If we are hungry, we might construct a memory of a cafe we saw on our walk two weeks ago. If we have a fight with our partner, we might suddenly remember all the times they disappointed us, when we usually are able to accept their imperfections.

When Emily became a parent, her goals changed dramatically, and it changed what memories her brain predicted might be useful for her.

Articles that explore holiday stress management, managing conflict, picking gifts, making resolutions, and more.

Sources indicate that emily realized that her experience of being her son’s age was one of bracing and zoning out because she had felt disconnected from her mother and scared of her father at the time. As a parent, Emily was suddenly able to attune to what it felt like for her to be three years old. Her three-year-old self did not feel safe, and she did not believe her child was safe, either.

Sources indicate that conway notes that the memories we are able to construct have to be coherent with how we think of ourselves, our beliefs about ourselves, and the world and people in it. According to Conway’s theory, our brains filter, rationalize, or dismiss memories that are inconsistent with who we believe we are.

In a recent development, before Emily had children, she believed, largely unconsciously, that her childhood experiences were irrelevant to who she was and that she hadn’t really been affected by them. When she became a mum, her visceral memories of childhood fear did not match up with who she believed she was anymore. Her goals had changed from surviving and rationalizing to tuning in to and protecting her child. Her brain was telling her she had to shield her child from something that she had experienced as frightening as a child.

Industry observers note that other clients of mine have found that becoming a parent had the opposite effect. They were able to look at the younger versions of their parents with more compassion and kindness, reconstructing memories through the eyes of an exhausted parent who was trying and barely coping.

Sources indicate that karen and her parents had had a difficult relationship. Karen’s parents divorced when she was young, and Karen had always felt her mother had been unavailable when she was a child. She experienced a lot of anger when thinking about her childhood. She had memories of having to take on responsibilities too early, looking after her siblings, and cooking and cleaning while her mother was at work. Karen had purposefully moved away from her parents and had spent years asserting her independence. She had never wanted children because she had such strong memories of what it had been like to be a young caretaker and not being able to feel like a child. When she met her husband, she realized that creating her own family was more key to her than she had thought.

Karen came to see me for anxiety. She was worried about losing her freedom when she became a mother, and we thought about how her childhood experiences shaped her experience now. I saw Karen for quite some time after she gave birth, and something shifted for her when she became a parent. She remembered instances of seeing her mother frazzled, rushed, and overwhelmed and how hard she had tried to find time to be there for Karen and her siblings. Karen started to realize how impossible it must have been for her mother to raise three children on her own while working.

Industry observers note that karen tried to talk to her mother and learned about how ashamed she was for burdening her daughter and unsure about whether Karen wanted her in her life. To her surprise, Karen experienced her mother’s relationship with her own daughter as reparative. She could make sense of her anger and her need for freedom and see that what happened in her childhood was not something her mother had intended.

In a recent development, for Emily, too, her experiences meant she had to rebuild the relationship with her mother and find a more honest foundation. She was able to have conversations with her about what it would have been like for Emily growing up, and, to Emily’s surprise, her mother also listened and apologized for not having checked in with her sooner. It started a healing process for Emily that involved listening to what her three-year-old self might have felt and acknowledging that she had been trying to rationalize her way out of feeling for most of her life. She had to slowly let herself experience that her parents were safe now; she decided to not rely on them for child care but let the relationship grow more slowly.

It has been revealed that what helped Emily was hearing her mother validate what happened to her as a child. It was something Emily would have needed when she was younger. She was also able to make upcoming meaning of her relationship with her parents through therapy—an act of shared social construction with another human, the therapist, that fulfills some of our core needs of being heard, seen, and understood.

Karen similarly needed to feel heard by her mother. Her anger dissipated when she was able to put herself into her mother’s shoes and see that her and her mother’s experience could exist side by side.

What can you do if parenthood is shifting your relationship with your own parents? Here are steps that I have found are helpful for my clients.

Find support. The first step in coping with a difficult experience is to not try to go through it alone. We are social beings who need to feel understood by others. Seek out a friend or a sibling if you are struggling with feelings you do not understand.

Industry observers note that meet yourself with self-compassion. When strong emotions come up, we might tell ourselves, “I’m overreacting,” “I’m too sensitive,” “I just need to get on with things and stop complaining.” Self-criticism can perpetuate a cycle in which we invalidate our experiences until they become impossible to ignore. It also won’t help to be overly critical of yourself if you believe you’ve been judging your parents too harshly, now that you have the perspective of being a parent yourself.

Recent findings suggest that seek out conversations. If thinking back on your childhood memories brings up a perspective change on your childhood, speak to your family, your parents or siblings, and learn about how they experienced that time and you as a child. It might help you feel more compassion with your parents who may have been struggling, and can also help you understand yourself better as a person.

Set boundaries, if needed. If memories from your childhood suddenly take on latest meaning, it might be crucial to think about boundaries and clear rules to set with your child’s grandparents. If you felt unsafe or uncomfortable as a child, it is OK to make it clear how you expect the adults in your child’s life to behave. This can, of course, be easier stated than done, and it can be useful to seek help to deal with feelings of guilt or anxiety around setting boundaries with your parents.

Recent findings suggest that seek out professional help. Remember that every experience is subjective—your version of what happened might be different from that of your siblings or your parents. That does not make it any less valid. While Emily was lucky that her mother acknowledged her experience, your family members might not always be so receptive and might be more defensive about any wrongdoing. Seeking professional help can be especially useful when you are dealing with a family system that is less likely to take responsibility or want to change.

Recent findings suggest that becoming a parent changes your world in a thousand ways and can dramatically alter the way you look at your own childhood. Self-compassion is hugely vital in navigating all the transformations you might go through as a upcoming parent. Finding others that meet you with understanding and care is the first step in making sure you can meet yourself and your child in the same way.

*The stories in this article are a combination of experiences of several clients; any identifying information has been changed.

Sarah Emmerson, PsychD, is a chartered counseling psychologist and cofounder of Talking Women, a private psychology practice in London specializing in women's mental health.

#103782. Necessary Losses: The Life-Shaping Art of Letting Go

Necessary Losses: The Life-Shaping Art of Letting Go

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (910 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Themarginalian

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “The art of losing isn’t hard to master,” Elizabeth Bishop wrote in one of the great masterpieces of poetry.
  • We dream of immortality because we are creatures made of loss — the death of the individual is what ensured the survival of the species along the evolutionary vector of adaptation — and made for loss: All of our creativity, all of our compulsive productivity, all of our poems and our space telescopes, are but a coping mechanism for our mortality, for the elemental knowledge that we will lose everything and everyone we cherish as we inevitably return our borrowed stardust to the universe.
  • And yet the measure of life, the meaning of it, may be precisely what we make of our losses — how we turn the dust of disappointment and dissolution into clay for creation and self-creation, how we make of loss a reason to love more fully and live more deeply.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“The art of losing isn’t hard to master,” Elizabeth Bishop wrote in one of the great masterpieces of poetry. “Every mortal loss is an Immortal Gain,” William Blake wrote two centuries before her in his beautiful letter to a bereaved father.

We dream of immortality because we are creatures made of loss — the death of the individual is what ensured the survival of the species along the evolutionary vector of adaptation — and made for loss: All of our creativity, all of our compulsive productivity, all of our poems and our space telescopes, are but a coping mechanism for our mortality, for the elemental knowledge that we will lose everything and everyone we cherish as we inevitably return our borrowed stardust to the universe.

And yet the measure of life, the meaning of it, may be precisely what we make of our losses — how we turn the dust of disappointment and dissolution into clay for creation and self-creation, how we make of loss a reason to love more fully and live more deeply.

That is what Judith Viorst explores in her 1987 consolation of a book Necessary Losses (public library) — an inquiry into the profound and far-reaching relationship between our losses and our gains, revealing renunciation as a fulcrum of growth. She paints the vast landscape of loss upon which life plays out:.

When we think of loss we think of the loss, through death, of people we love. But loss is a far more encompassing theme in our life. For we lose not only through death, but also by leaving and being left, by changing and letting go and moving on. And our losses include not only our separations and departures from those we love, but our conscious and unconscious losses of romantic dreams, impossible expectations, illusions of freedom and power, illusions of safety — and the loss of our own younger self, the self that thought it always would be unwrinkled and invulnerable and immortal.

These necessary losses… we confront when we are confronted by the inescapable fact… that we are essentially out here on our own; that we will have to accept — in other people and ourselves — the mingling of love with hate, of the good with the bad;… that there are flaws in every human connection; that our status on this planet is implacably impermanent; and that we are utterly powerless to offer ourselves or those we love protection — protection from danger and pain, from the in-roads of time, from the coming of age, from the coming of death; protection from our necessary losses.

According to recent reports, these losses are a part of life — universal, unavoidable, inexorable. And these losses are necessary because we grow by losing and leaving and letting go.

In a recent development, as a sculpture is shaped by what is chiseled off from the block of stone, so too are we shaped by what we lose — by choice, with all the complexities and difficulties of letting go, or by the scythe of chance, which takes away as impartially as it gives. Viorst writes:.

The road to human development is paved with renunciation. Throughout our life we grow by giving up. We give up some of our deepest attachments to others. We give up certain cherished parts of ourselves. We must confront, in the dreams we dream, as well as in our intimate relationships, all that we never will have and never will be. Passionate investment leaves us vulnerable to loss. And sometimes, no matter how clever we are, we must lose… It is only through our losses that we become fully developed human beings.

We enter the realm of loss the moment the umbilical cord is cut to sever what Viorst calls the “blurred-boundary bliss of mother-child oneness” — the primal loss that sets off the ongoing task of becoming ourselves. From this origin point, she traces the lifelong vector of losses and gains:.

It has been revealed that exchanging the illusion of absolute shelter and absolute safety for the triumphant anxieties of standing alone… we become a moral, responsible, adult self, discovering — within the limitations imposed by necessity — our freedoms and choices. And in giving up our impossible expectations, we become a lovingly connected self, renouncing ideal visions of perfect friendship, marriage, children, family life for the sweet imperfections of all-too-human relationships. And in confronting the many losses that are brought by time and death, we become a mourning and adapting self, finding at every stage — until we draw our final breath — opportunities for creative transformations.

In a sentiment the poet Mark Doty would echo — “you need to both remember where love leads and love anyway,” he wrote in his beautiful reckoning with love and loss — she adds:.

We cannot deeply love anything without becoming vulnerable to loss. And we cannot become separate people, responsible people, connected people, reflective people without some losing and leaving and letting go.

Complement Necessary Losses, which goes on to explore the many regions of loss in human life and how they can become frontiers of growth, with Hannah Arendt on learning how to live with the fundamental fear of loss, Thoreau on living through a loss, and Alan Watts on learning not to think of gain and loss, then explore two uncommon lenses on loss: fractals and chlorophyll.
